vignette:
Dr. Imani Adebayo carries herself with an unnerving stillness. At twenty-one, she is the youngest surgical resident in the program, a prodigy who completed her medical training back home with a speed that left her professors alternately awestruck and concerned. Here, her colleagues see only the brilliance. They see the preternatural calm in the operating room, the elegant efficiency of her hands, and the quiet, almost severe, focus she brings to every case. They don’t see the effort it takes to keep her hands from trembling when she scrubs in, a tremor so fine it’s more a memory of motion than a physical reality.

It has been ten months since the rains came. Not the usual seasonal downpour, but something malevolent and alive. Imani was on a 36-hour shift at the teaching hospital when the river broke its banks. She speaks of it in fragments, her voice losing its crisp, professional cadence and becoming flat, distant. The first sign was the water seeping under the doors of the ground-floor emergency department, brown and foul-smelling. Then the power failed, plunging the windowless corridors into a terrifying, humid darkness, broken only by the beams of flashlights and phones.

The hospital, a place of order, became a chaotic island. Imani, who had only just begun her internship, was suddenly one of the most senior medical personnel on the flooded floors. She describes the night with a detached, sensory precision: the slick film of mud on every surface, the constant, panicked shouting echoing in the stairwells, the low groan of the building settling. She worked for two days straight, suturing wounds by the light of a phone, setting fractures with improvised splints, and triaging patients in a hallway as the water lapped at the gurneys.

The memory that breaks through this detached narrative is that of a small boy, no older than seven, with a crush injury to his leg from a collapsed wall. She had him on a makeshift table in what was once a supply closet. The air was thick with the coppery smell of blood and the stench of the floodwater. She did everything she could, everything her training had prepared her for, but she had no blood bank, no surgical suite, no electricity for the monitors. She remembers pressing her hands against the wound, feeling the boy’s life draining away into the murky water that covered the floor. She can still feel the chilling warmth, and she remembers looking down at her own hands, stained and useless, as the boy went quiet.

Afterward, the fellowship in this new country felt like an escape, a lifeline. It was a testament to the work she had done, a reward for her survival. But the escape was an illusion. The trauma followed her across the ocean, embedding itself in the very environment that was meant to be her sanctuary. The sterile smell of the hospital now mixes with the phantom scent of mud and decay. The rhythmic beep of a cardiac monitor can suddenly become the sound of the failing backup generator. A sudden downpour outside the hospital window can leave her breathless, her heart pounding against her ribs as she stares at the water streaming down the glass.

She works relentlessly, taking on extra shifts, burying herself in research. Her colleagues praise her dedication, her insatiable work ethic. They don’t understand that she is running. She cannot sleep for more than a few hours before the dreams begin—the rising water, the boy’s wide, trusting eyes. She avoids social invitations, finding superficial conversation unbearable. The world outside the hospital feels flimsy, unreal. In the OR, under the bright, sterile lights, she can almost feel in control. But then she’ll look down at her gloved hands, poised over a patient, and for a terrifying second, she is back in the dark, the water rising around her ankles, and the only thing she can feel is failure.
